subject: physics
title: Weight
summary: Weight is the force of gravity pulling on an object's mass — measured in newtons, and it changes depending on where you are. Your 45 kg body has the same mass everywhere, but weighs about 441 N on Earth, only 73 N on the Moon, and nothing at all while floating free. Explore how a spring scale reads this force on different worlds.

plainLanguageExplanation: Weight is a force: the gravity pull acting on an object's mass. Because it's a force, weight has units of newtons and, like all forces, can change. The famous formula is weight = mass × g, where g is the strength of gravity in that place — about 9.8 m/s² on Earth, 1.6 on the Moon. So a 5 kg rock: 5 × 9.8 = 49 N on Earth, but 5 × 1.6 = 8 N on the Moon. The rock is still 5 kg of matter — its mass never changed — what changed is the force pulling on it. In the model you hang objects from a spring scale, which stretches exactly in proportion to the pull; read the newton mark, then spin the location dial and watch the needle fall (or float to zero in space). Weight is what your body feels, why 'weight loss' happens on a space station, and why you can jump six times as high on the Moon.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: The gravitational force acting on an object's mass

keyFacts.label: Unit
keyFacts.value: Newtons (N) — it's a force, not a kilogram

keyFacts.label: Formula
keyFacts.value: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg)

keyFacts.label: Earth's g
keyFacts.value: About 9.8 m/s², so a 10 kg object weighs ≈ 98 N

keyFacts.label: On the Moon
keyFacts.value: g ≈ 1.6, so the same object weighs about 1/6 as much

keyFacts.label: Not mass
keyFacts.value: Mass stays the same everywhere; weight depends on where you are

whyItMatters: Weight is the force you actually feel every moment — your scale at the doctor's, the heaviness of a backpack, the strain on a bridge's cables. Engineers design for weight (a force that changes with place) and for mass (which stays fixed), and getting the pair straight is the difference between a safe bridge and a sagging one. Weight also explains everyday wonders: why astronauts float, why your ears pop in a fast elevator, and why Moon-jumping is effortless.
didYouKnow: Because weight is a force and mass is not, a bathroom scale on the Moon would still say '5 kg' if it were actually measuring force and converting — but on a space station, your weight reads zero while your mass remains perfectly normal. You don't lose mass in orbit, you lose weight.
compareReason: The spring-scale needle that falls on the Moon while the kg plaque stays fixed is the cleanest picture of weight (force, changes) versus mass (matter, constant).
